items.title: The Longest Theatrical Runs in Film History
items.summary: A story with universal themes. Characters who are endlessly quotable. Not every movie has achieved the record-breaking longevity of the ones on this list, with theatrical runs lasting a year or even decades. The movies that did earn this popularity were more than just crowd-pleasers, too. One is a Bollywood rom-com with lifelong fans. Another has roaring dinosaurs breaking free of their cages. An accomplishment they all share, no matter how different they are in genre or story, is how they made a mark in pop culture. Let’s check out the movies that have spent the most time in theaters. E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial (1982) Time in theaters: 52 Weeks ‘E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial’ (1982)Credit: Universal Pictures The legacy of this Steven Spielberg-directed film is still going strong; just look at how it influenced Stranger Things. More than that, E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial told the sweet story of a boy who befriends a lost alien, with scenes and a score by John Williams that were full of imagination. It stayed in theaters for almost a whole year after its release in June 1982. But the biggest achievement was that it earned the rare box office record that still hasn’t been beaten: E.T. was in the weekend Top 10 for 44 weeks. And it wouldn’t be the only film by Spielberg to be such a hit with moviegoers. Jurassic Park (1993) Time in theaters: 70 Weeks ‘Jurassic Park’ (1993)Credit: Universal Pictures The epic score by John Williams and the groundbreaking CGI to bring the dinos to life have made Jurassic Park a spectacle. The prehistoric creatures felt as real as the human cast. More spectacular than either of those sights or sounds was the staying power. Eleven years after Steven Spielberg’s enormous success with E.T., he gave audiences another summer blockbuster to rush to see at their local cinemas. items.title: Iconic Film Introductions: Anton Chigurh’s First Few Minutes Are a Masterclass in Fear
items.summary: One of the most chilling performances of the 21st century is Javier Bardem’s turn as serial killer Anton Chigurh in the Best Picture winner, No Country for Old Men. The film dissects the nature of evil and the cynicism of human nature through the film’s narration, combined with his performance. Let’s take a look at the opening sequence of the film and why Bardem’s introduction has always stuck with us. Tommy Lee Jones’ Narration Throughout the film, Tommy Lee Jones’ Ed Tom Bell chimes in to narrate his troubles and thoughts about the world. These monologues are plucked from Cormac McCarthy’s original novel, and in the opening scene as Chigurh is arrested and placed in a squad car alongside his CO2 canister weapon, we get our first instance of this. He talks about a young man he arrested and sent to the electric chair who bragged about the murder he committed, would absolutely commit more, and that he was anticipating going to hell. Ed knew not what to make of that. It’s in this moment where we quickly realize that Anton Chigurh is about to be depicted as the version of that young man who was never caught. The one who mysteriously always evaded capture, a proper identity beyond a name, a motivation for his crimes, and any ounce of regret. Chigurh’s face is hidden in the shadows even when shot from the front during this narration to emphasize his mythical nature that will be echoed throughout the entire film. Even when he is known by other characters, his elusiveness allows him to blend right in. The Presence of the Score ‘No Country for Old Men’Credit: Miramax/Paramount Pictures No Country for Old Men famously lacks a musical score almost entirely. The Coen Brothers were very particular about making sure the unpredictable nature of the film was emphasized, and that every moment of emotion lacked a sense of manufacturing via musical intervention. items.title: 10 Years Before 'Iron Man', This R-Rated Marvel Movie Changed Superhero Cinema
items.summary: 2008’s Iron Man is often credited with establishing the modern boom of superhero movies. While the blockbuster was indeed a zeitgeist-defining hit that kicked off the Marvel Cinematic Universe (which is now the highest-grossing film franchise of all time with a cumulative worldwide box office gross of more than $32 billion), it arrived in a cinematic landscape that had already been primed to receive such a movie thanks to a much earlier hit: 1998’s Blade. The movie, which starred Wesley Snipes as Marvel Comics’ titular half-vampire vampire hunter, cleanly split the American superhero genre into pre-Blade and post-Blade eras. Let’s break down exactly how that happened. The Superhero Genre Before Blade Comic book superheroes have been hitting theaters in various forms basically since the invention of cinema. Very early on, exhibitors realized that the big screen needs big spectacle, from the special effects magic of Georges Méliès to the sweeping grandeur of D. W. Griffith’s Intolerance. In the 1930s, superheroes took the stage largely in the form of film serials adapting comic strip characters like Dick Tracy and Flash Gordon. Superhero comics as we know them didn’t launch until the late 1930s, but 1940s film serials quickly brought in recognizable comic book characters including Superman and Batman after their respective introductions. When the film serial format died out, serialized storytelling moved to the burgeoning art form of television, which is where superheroes thrived in the 1960s and 1970s with shows like Batman, Wonder Woman, and The Incredible Hulk. The genre shifted back to the big screen once more when 1978’s Superman swept into theaters after George Lucas’ 1977 sci-fi megahit Star Wars proved that there was a strong appetite for big-budget, special-effects-driven sci-fi titles. items.title: Applications Are Open for This Filmmaker Sabbatical in Colorado
items.summary: Rest is not a word the film industry uses much. It's the entire premise of the Ouray Film Sabbatical, a four-day, fully funded residency in the San Juan Mountains that just announced its 2027 facilitator lineup. The dates are Jan. 7-10, 2027, in Ouray, Colorado, which is a tiny town tucked into a canyon that markets itself as the "Little Switzerland of America." The sabbatical is a spinoff of the Ouray International Film Festival, now heading into its seventh year. OIFF has built a reputation as a filmmaker-first fest, and the sabbatical extends that ethos beyond the festival's four-day annual run. The sabbatical is all about rest, community, and being in the same room with people who do what you do to have time to play and recuperate. Applications are open through Oct. 5. Learn more below. Why It's Different from the Usual Lab Most opportunities you'll find on our seasonal grants and fellowships roundups are structured around a project. You bring a script, a rough cut, or a pitch. You leave with notes and a way forward. Ouray is doing something else. Co-founder Benjamin Wiessner (who received the SXSW Janet Pierson Champion Award in 2026) said of the program: “We started this initiative to provide unsiloed support for mid-career film workers, giving them an opportunity to be cared for, truly listened to, and asked the simple questions at the right time that can spark their own transformation. I am so thrilled about the terrific humans we have as facilitators for the sabbatical. In addition to their incredible bona fides, these people are also creating new space for film and film workers by thinking about and building for others.” In a Short of the Week piece on the inaugural 2026 cohort, Jake Abell, another co-founder of the sabbatical, said, "Nobody's talking about rest, apart from as a cry for help." items.title: DesView Introduces Its New Flagship-Grade Wireless Video Transmission System With Insane Range
items.summary: A new wireless transmission system from the team at Desview is here, angling to be a top option for filmmakers and crews looking to add reliable wireless video transmission to their productions. This new system is set to consist of a wireless transmitter and receiver set that will be able to provide HDMI input and output with 5 GHz line-of-sight transmission from a pretty remarkable 1300’ away. The promise is to provide all of this with reliability and low latency, and to allow crews to work with efficient H.264 encoding and decoding of up to 1080p60 video. Pretty bold claims and exciting stuff; let’s check it out. The Desview Thunderbolt 1080p Wireless Transmission System Overall, while there are many wireless video transmission systems currently on the market, there is always room for more to help keep competition high and, hopefully, costs low. This new Thunderbolt 1080p wireless transmission system from Desview should help with both, as it has a receiver with dual HDMI outputs and a transmitter with an HDMI loop output for displaying your local feed on a monitor. The system is set to be compatible with lower resolutions, along with the higher 1080p60 video specs mentioned above, and it should be able to provide low 60 ms latency, which should further help ensure all your transmissions are clear and free of blur. What’s neat about this system is that its HDMI output port on the transmitter allows video to be displayed on a monitor without compromising the quality of the transmitted signal. Price and Availability This new system shows promise, as it appears to be both reliable and convenient in design. The units are also HDCP-compliant to help ensure there's no copyright blocking on your transmissions, and the system can automatically choose a high-quality frequency channel with its invisible smart channel-hopping feature, which works in real time. items.title: ARRI’s LiOS Software Gets Major Update Bringing Enhanced DMX Live View Functionality
items.summary: Big news for those interested in high-end lighting for their film and video projects, as ARRI has announced that the latest update for the company’s Lighting Operating System (LiOS) software is out. This latest update, version 3.3.0, is set to enhance the DMX Live View functionality and introduce helpful new smoothing for DMX Zone Modes. This update should add smoother, more consistent lighting controls throughout and provide other system improvements. Here’s what you need to know. ARRI LiOS 3.3.0 Update This latest update to the ARRI LiOS software is here and should be quite intriguing for anyone currently, or perhaps in the future, looking to use the SkyPanel Pro, SkyPanel X, or Orbiter. This firmware update is set to enhance the DMX Live View functionality and introduce smoothing for DMX Zone Modes, which should provide smoother, more consistent lighting control. The update is also set to fix various reported issues and bugs, as well as provide your general mix of system improvements that should boost reliability and performance. Here’s the full list of what’s new in LiOS 3.3.0: Enhanced DMX Live View functionality Smoothing for DMX Zone Modes Further reliability improvements and bug fixes The company further recommends that all users update to the latest LiOS 3.3.0 version. Also, please note that due to the significant changes introduced in LiOS 3.1, downgrading to versions prior to LiOS 3.1 is not possible at this time. If you’d like more info, you can read the full update report and access all the files on the company’s website here.

items.title: Why Is There So Much Junk Food in 'Teenage Sex & Death at Camp Miasma'?
items.summary: On Saturday night, I grabbed a big bag of gummy bears and settled in for a really cool horror and sex deconstruction from Jane Schoenbrun’s Teenage Sex & Death at Camp Miasma. If you saw it this weekend, you probably walked away with both the brilliant deconstruction of '80s slasher movies and a sudden, irresistible urge to buy even more junk food on the way out. One of the major themes of the movie is the idea of junk food, comfort, and movies, all intertwined. In fact, one of the best scenes is when director Kris (Hannah Einbinder) is munching on Raisinets and popcorn in bed to the eye-catching visual of a chandelier made entirely out of candy wrappers. At first glance, you might brush it off as typical indie film quirky set dressing, but in true Schoenbrun fashion, every motif serves a deeper emotional function. So what’s actually going on with all that candy? - YouTubewww.youtube.com Comfort Food as an Emotional Safety Net In a recent interview with Deadline, Schoenbrun opened up about how all that junk food ended up in the movie and why it’s intimately tied to their themes of trauma, vulnerability, and intimacy. They said: DEADLINE: I’m curious about the symbolism of all the processed junk food and the chandelier of wrappers. SCHOENBRUN: The junk food in the movie, I forget when it found its way in there. It’s like so much of the movie is about, like I said, ritual, about being in a mindset where you can really enjoy something scary, whether that be Kris [Hannah Einbinder] in bed, with, you know, with Raisinets and the popcorn, watching a schlocky horror movie, or the two characters learning how to be present and enjoy sex after a lot of trauma. There is this idea that if it gets too real, you can turn it off, that you’re exploring something dangerous, doing it in a way that’s actually safe. items.title: Read 'The Odyssey' Screenplay
items.summary: The biggest hit of the year, so far, is The Odyssey, which rocketed past a billion dollars worldwide today and will probably top off somewhere around $1.5 billion, making it Nolan's top-grossing film ever and solidifying it as one of the top-grossing movies this year. As with any movie, it starts with a screenplay. This one is an adaptation of Homer's epic, where Nolan read a few translations of the work, as well as the Aeneid, Iliad, and other poems, in order to add some details to the story. It will surely be in the conversation for the Best Adapted Screenplay Academy Award. Today, we're proud to link you to The Odyssey screenplay. As always, this is for educational purposes only. Lessons From The Odyssey Screenplay The core of any successful adaptation is a thematic anchor that grounds the whole idea in something that stays tangible for the audience. In this movie, it's Xenia, or Zeus's law, which is the hospitality rule that the Greeks are supposed to follow. While the whole movie is sort of an exploration of home, identity, and the price of hubris, all that gets summed up in how people treat their guests one stop after another on the journey home. Of course, Nolan was never going to tell this story in a straightforward way. He loves these fractured timelines that blend the years that are passing in the past and present. We have grounded markers like the aging dog to help us, but the narrative opens in media res with the telling of Odysseus's story and then flashes to the aftermath of the king's absence. Every storyline has propulsion. Odysseus is trying to remember one, trying to get home in a boat, and you also have Telemachus’s active search for news of his father. That urgency sustains the page length and keeps us excited, although I think Nolan's name on the script would help, versus if you or I turned in a 175-page screenplay. items.title: Film Quote of the Day: The Line from Clint Eastwood’s 1993 Classic That Still Feels True Today
items.summary: I fI could pick one actor to deliver something I wrote, it'd be hard to pick against prime Clint Eastwood. The guy has spoken some all-time lines, from Dirty Harry’s "Do you feel lucky, punk?" to Unforgiven’s "Deserves got nothing to do with it." His characters and their voices stand the pantheon of time. And here's another sneaky thing: he makes sure that in the movies he directs, even the characters he doesn't play get their moment to shine, too. One of those hidden gem movies that not enough of us talk about is his 1993 movie A Perfect World, which sticks out like a beacon of light in a genre usually defined by darkness. Even its tragic ending has this hopeful twinge that sucks us in. More than thirty years after its release, this film has Eastwood’s most complex thematic statements all contained in a line that punctuates a fun part of the movie. Let's dive into the quote. - YouTubewww.youtube.com The Scene in Question This is one of my favorite movies to recommend to people because I feel like it has all these moral lessons and quandaries within it that people really enjoy, and also has this poignant end that gets them talking afterward. A Perfect World follows escaped convict Butch Haynes (Kevin Costner) as he evades a massive statewide manhunt led by Texas Ranger Red Garnett (Clint Eastwood). Along the way, Butch takes an eight-year-old Jehovah’s Witness boy named Phillip (T.J. Lowther) hostage and shows him the world. The movie takes place across the sun-drenched backroads of 1963 Texas. It's those sunny vistas and long stretches of highway that allow our hero and his kidnapper to form a bond around the broken world. Philip's life was sheltered, and he's never gotten to do anything he's wanted to do, or anything like a normal kid. Case in point, he's never been trick-or-treating.
